terms.grammar: adjective, the participle of adolēscō; as a noun, a grown-up
terms.comment: From adolēscō, “grow up”. Traupman gives adultus homō for an adult (Traupman 269).

evidence: Caes. BG 5.56.2: omnēs pūberēs armātī convenīre cōnsuērunt
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: grown-up persons, adults, men. Festus puts the age at fourteen for a boy and twelve for a girl.

terms.gloss: grown-ups, as against children; one’s elders
evidence: Aug. Conf. 1.9.15: majōrum nūgae negōtia vocantur
terms.comment: In classical prose majōrēs nātū are one’s elders, and majōrēs alone usually one’s ancestors; Augustine uses it for the grown-ups of a child’s world.

phrases.latin: sed majōrum nūgae negōtia vocantur, puerōrum autem tālia cum sint, pūniuntur ā majōribus
phrases.english: but grown-ups’ games are called business, and when children play the same games, the grown-ups punish them

phrases.latin: ex quō togam virīlem sūmpsit nūllō diē prius ūllam pūblicam prīvātamque rem ēgit quam in Capitōlium īret
phrases.english: from the day he came of age, he never did any business, public or private, without first going up to the Capitol

sources: Lewis & Short: adolesco · Lewis & Short: pubes · Lewis & Short: major
